content: The WHO Secretariat provided essential guidance throughout the development of the guidelines. The Guidelines Review Committee offered critical feedback, which was incorporated into the final version of the document. WHO also acknowledges the contributions of those who prepared existing guidance on lymphatic filariasis (LF) and mass drug administration (MDA) for neglected tropical diseases, as well as academic researchers who conducted studies to improve treatment regimens aimed at eliminating LF as a public health problem. These resources formed the foundation for the preparation of the new guideline. External partners did not contribute to the development of this guideline. Funding for the guideline was generously provided by the United States Agency for International Development (USAID). However, the development and content of the guideline were completed independently of the funder. Lymphatic filariasis (LF) is a vector-borne neglected tropical disease that damages the lymphatic system, leading to conditions such as lymphedema (elephantiasis) and hydrocele in affected individuals. Globally, it is estimated that 25 million men suffer from hydrocele, and over 15 million people experience lymphedema. At least 36 million individuals live with these chronic manifestations. LF causes disfigurement, disability, stigma, and poverty, with hundreds of millions of dollars lost annually due to reduced productivity among affected patients. WHO has identified LF as one of the leading causes of permanent and long-term disability worldwide. In 1997, the Fiftieth World Health Assembly resolved to eliminate LF as a public health problem. WHO launched the Global Programme to Eliminate Lymphatic Filariasis (GPELF) in 2000, aiming to achieve global elimination by 2020. The strategy includes annual MDA to interrupt transmission and morbidity management to alleviate suffering. To date, 7 billion cumulative treatments have been delivered to over 850 million people in 66 of the 72 endemic countries. At least 20 countries are now under post-MDA surveillance to confirm elimination. However, 22 endemic countries have not yet started MDA in all implementation units, and some countries face challenges with suboptimal assessment results despite completing five effective MDA rounds. Consequently, global elimination by 2020 is no longer feasible with existing regimens. This guideline responds to requests from countries for alternative regimens to realign their national programs toward elimination. WHO evaluated evidence on alternative regimens and employed a rigorous guideline development process to recommend new approaches for LF elimination. Two alternative MDA regimens were considered: (1) a three-drug regimen (ivermectin, diethylcarbamazine, and albendazole) instead of the current two-drug regimens, and (2) biannual MDA with the current two-drug regimens instead of annual MDA. Recommendations were formulated based on the GRADE approach, considering factors such as the priority of the problem, benefits and harms, evidence quality, resource implications, equity, acceptability, and feasibility. The guideline outlines the context, methodology, and recommendations for alternative regimens, as well as WHO’s plans for dissemination, implementation, and monitoring. It is intended to assist decision-makers in endemic countries in determining if, when, and how to use alternative MDA regimens. The target audience includes national program coordinators, technical groups, and stakeholders supporting GPELF, such as health ministries, WHO, donors, NGOs, and academic institutions. The guideline emphasizes the importance of respecting human rights and addressing the needs of socially marginalized individuals affected by LF. The recommendations focus specifically on MDA for LF elimination and do not cover other public health interventions, such as morbidity management, vector control, or health education, which are addressed in separate WHO publications.
